findings.title: Errors on 5 fields are not announced to screen readers
findings.meaning: After submitting the form with its required fields empty, 5 fields give a screen reader no error: "Pet name" (not marked invalid (no aria-invalid="true") and its error message is not linked to it (aria-describedby) and nothing is announced in a live region); "Pet type" (not marked invalid (no aria-invalid="true") and its error message is not linked to it (aria-describedby) and nothing is announced in a live region); "Start date" (not marked invalid (no aria-invalid="true") and its error message is not linked to it (aria-describedby) and nothing is announced in a live region); "End date" (not marked invalid (no aria-invalid="true") and its error message is not linked to it (aria-describedby) and nothing is announced in a live region); "Owner email" (not marked invalid (no aria-invalid="true") and its error message is not linked to it (aria-describedby) and nothing is announced in a live region). The errors may be visible on screen, but a screen reader user is not told which fields have a problem or what it is.
findings.impact: Blind and low-vision users submit the form, nothing seems to happen, and they can't find out what to fix, so they can't complete the form.
findings.fix: When "Pet name", "Pet type", "Start date", "End date" and "Owner email" fail validation, set aria-invalid="true" on each field, point its aria-describedby at the error message element, and announce a summary in a polite live region (role="status") or move focus to the first invalid field.

findings.title: Secret key shipped to every visitor: an AI provider secret key (sk-…)
findings.meaning: The page's JavaScript contains an AI provider secret key (sk-…). Anything in the page's scripts can be read by anyone who opens the site, so this key is effectively public. It was found in http://localhost:3160/config/ai-client.js (line 6).
findings.impact: Anyone can copy the key and use it as you: run up bills on your account, read or change your data, or bypass your security rules.
findings.fix: Remove the key from the frontend code and move the call that needs it to your server (or an edge function). Then revoke the key and create a new one, because the old one has already been exposed.

findings.title: The server returns a stack trace in its error response
3 security header problems (Content-Security-Policy, Clickjacking protection, X-Content-Type-Options)
findings.meaning: The page's response is missing protections that browsers only apply when the server asks for them: Content-Security-Policy missing; Clickjacking protection (frame-ancestors or X-Frame-Options) missing; X-Content-Type-Options missing.
findings.impact: Without them, nothing limits which scripts the page may run, so a single injected script (XSS) can do anything a signed-in user can; and any website can load this page in an invisible frame and trick people into clicking its buttons (clickjacking); and browsers may guess a file's type, so an uploaded or user-supplied file can be run as a script.
findings.fix: Ask your AI or developer: "Send these response headers on every page (in the server, framework config or hosting config): Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; frame-ancestors 'self'; X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. Check the app still loads its scripts, styles and API calls with the new Content-Security-Policy."

findings.title: Session cookie "kennel_session" has no HttpOnly
findings.meaning: "kennel_session": any script on the page can read it.
findings.impact: A session cookie is the key to someone's account. If a script can read it, one injected script (XSS) can steal every visitor's session and sign in as them.
findings.fix: Ask your AI or developer: "Set the session cookie "kennel_session" from the server with HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Secure (Secure in production). Never write session tokens with document.cookie or keep them in localStorage."

findings.title: 2 endpoints let any website read them with the visitor's cookies
findings.meaning: Asked from a sandboxed frame (Origin: null, which any website can produce), the app answered with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. The browser therefore lets every website read GET /api/__config, GET /api/bookings.
findings.impact: Any website a signed-in user visits can quietly call these endpoints with the user's cookies and read the answers: their data, their account details, anything the app returns.
findings.fix: Ask your AI or developer: "Our CORS setup trusts the 'null' origin (it echoes the request's Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true). Only allow our own front-end origins (an explicit list), never echo the request's Origin, never allow 'null', and only send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials for origins on that list."
